design_detail: Analysis of community drug-checking programme data, filed as cross-sectional because each sample was analysed once; the schema has no test-accuracy design. Eight harm-reduction sites (supervised consumption and overdose prevention sites) in Vancouver and Surrey, British Columbia, October 2018 to January 2020: samples checked at the point of care by FTIR (Bruker ALPHA or ALPHA-II) and BTNX benzodiazepine test strips (with fentanyl strips), and a convenience subset also tested at confirmatory laboratories (Health Canada Drug Analysis Service: qNMR or GC–MS with LC-QTOF/MS confirmation; BC Provincial Toxicology Centre: GC–MS). Two aims: the number and type of NPS benzodiazepines among confirmed samples, and the false-positive and false-negative rates of the point-of-care methods against confirmatory results.
can_establish: Which NPS benzodiazepines confirmatory laboratories found in 159 (and a further 383) drug-checking samples in the Vancouver area in 2018–2020, and how often the benzodiazepine strip and FTIR agreed with those results in the 153 verified samples without only typical benzodiazepines.
cannot_establish: How common NPS benzodiazepines were in the local drug supply (a convenience subset partly sent because of suspected benzodiazepine overdose), the strips' accuracy for typical benzodiazepines (6 samples), accuracy in the 1209 unverified samples, what made the 20 strip false positives react, or any effect on behaviour or overdose.

sample.recruitment: Samples, not people: drugs brought voluntarily to harm-reduction sites. Confirmatory samples were a convenience subset: drugs discarded or not reclaimed, sent at the client's request, or clinically suspicious for benzodiazepine overdose (for example prolonged unconsciousness unlike opioid toxicity alone); the laboratory was chosen by availability or by site (Methods, 2nd paragraph, p. 3; Fig. 1, p. 4).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Samples with both point-of-care tests (strip and FTIR) and a confirmatory result; six confirmed to contain only typical benzodiazepines were removed from the NPS-benzodiazepine accuracy analysis (Table 3 note, p. 5).
sample.demographics: Not collected; data were anonymous (Methods, 5th paragraph, p. 3). Expected drug was reported by the person: fentanyl 90, alprazolam 17, 'down' 12, unknown 13, and others (Table 1).
sample.attrition: Of 1368 samples with both point-of-care tests, 159 (11.6%, editors' calculation) had confirmatory results; the rest are outside the accuracy analysis. Fig. 1 gives 543 confirmatory samples, but 159 + 383 = 542.
sample.selection_effects: Verification was partial and non-random and included samples sent because of suspected benzodiazepine overdose, which can raise the share of positives and bias the strip's apparent sensitivity in either direction; people using voluntary services may differ from the wider market (authors' limitation, p. 7).

exposure.measurement: Point of care (Methods, pp. 2–3): FTIR with the TICTAC, Bruker pharmaceutical, SWGDRUG and an in-house library, then the sample dissolved in water and tested with BTNX Rapid Response single-drug benzodiazepine strips (oxazepam calibrator, cut-off 300 ng/mL, validated by the maker for 22 benzodiazepines in urine) and fentanyl strips; results combined. Confirmatory: PTC GC–MS against a calibration list (Supplemental Table 2, not read); DAS qNMR or GC–MS, with LC-QTOF/MS confirmation of a targeted fentanyl and benzodiazepine method (Supplemental Table 3, not read).
exposure.polysubstance: Table 2: of the 24 NPS-benzodiazepine-positive samples, 17 also contained fentanyl (one also carfentanil); others contained methamphetamine (10), caffeine (19), phenacetin (7), 4-ANPP, N-phenylpropanamide and melatonin (editors' count from Table 2).

comparison.controls: Confirmatory result: any NPS benzodiazepine by GC–MS, LC-MS or qNMR at either laboratory (Table 1 footnote). Of 7 NPS-benzodiazepine-positive samples sent to both laboratories, 5 were confirmed at both and 2 at only one (Methods, 2nd paragraph, p. 3).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to samples. Not measured or not reported: benzodiazepine amounts, what made the 20 strip false positives react, strip lot, dissolution, the fentanyl-strip results, and the laboratories' target lists (supplement not read).

outcomes.instruments: False-positive rate (false positives over all confirmed negatives) and false-negative rate (false negatives over all confirmed positives) for strips, FTIR and either method, against confirmatory results for NPS benzodiazepines (Table 3, p. 5).
outcomes.validity_norms: The strips are designed for urine metabolites of common benzodiazepines (oxazepam, nordiazepam), not for NPS benzodiazepines or dissolved drug (Limitations, p. 7). The authors present the accuracy values on the assumption of some ability of the strips to detect NPS benzodiazepines (p. 4).
outcomes.operationalization: Positive = strip or FTIR positive; true positive = confirmed NPS benzodiazepine; samples with only typical benzodiazepines removed.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported; point-of-care results were recorded before confirmatory testing.

analysis.effect_sizes: No confidence intervals are printed. Strips: 15 of 24 confirmed NPS-benzodiazepine samples positive (sensitivity 62.5%; editors' Wilson 95% CI 42.7–78.8%), false-negative rate 37.5%; 20 of 129 confirmed negatives positive, false-positive rate 15.5% (10.3–22.7%), specificity 84.5% (editors' calculation); detection 7 of 8 (87.5%) with flualprazolam, flubromazolam or flubromazepam and 8 of 16 (50.0%; 28.0–72.0%) with etizolam alone. FTIR: 2 of 24 detected (false-negative 91.7%), 5 of 129 false positives (3.9%). Either method: 17 of 24 detected (false-negative 29.2%), 23 of 129 false positives (17.8%) (Results › Point-of-care accuracy & error; Table 3).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned; ethics approval from the Providence Health Care/University of British Columbia Research Ethics Board.
analysis.selective_reporting: Fentanyl-strip results from the same testing are not reported. The confirmatory-only subset (383) is described for NPS benzodiazepines only. Supplementary Tables 1–3 (strip insert details, laboratory target lists) were not read.
analysis.power: No sample-size calculation; 24 confirmed positives give wide intervals (editors' calculation above), as the authors note for the small subsamples (p. 7).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In a convenience subset of 159 drug-checking samples, 24 (15.1%) contained NPS benzodiazepines, mostly etizolam, none expected by the person; 17 of the 24 also held fentanyl. Strips detected 15 of 24 and read positive in 20 of 129 samples with no benzodiazepine found; FTIR detected 2 of 24. Strips detected typical benzodiazepines in all six samples that had them.
interpretation_gap.claimed: On accuracy the authors are cautious: point-of-care methods showed “substantial false positive and false negative rates” and should be routinely paired with confirmatory testing (Abstract; Conclusions, p. 7), which the results support. The framing of a first sizeable outbreak with 6.3% positivity among confirmatory samples (Discussion, p. 6) describes a non-random, partly overdose-driven subset, not the market, as the authors acknowledge in their limitations.

timeline.event: Benzodiazepine strips added to the Vancouver drug-checking programme in October, after counterfeit alprazolam containing fentanyl but no benzodiazepine was found (Methods, p. 2).

Shapiro et al. (2020), a BC Centre on Substance Use report cited in the Methods: flualprazolam and flubromazolam detected by the strips at concentrations similar to alprazolam, etizolam only at higher concentrations; not read.
Sisco et al.: in water, the same maker's benzodiazepine strip reacted to diazepam, alprazolam, bromazolam and flubromazepam but not to etizolam at any concentration tried (0.01 to 0.5 mg/mL).

replication.where_it_stands: Lower detection of etizolam is supported by the later laboratory study, which found no reaction at all; that half of the etizolam-only street samples were strip-positive here suggests other reacting compounds, untargeted benzodiazepines or lot differences, which neither paper resolves. The 15.5% false-positive rate has no independent estimate in the papers read.

funding.funder: Health Canada Substance Use and Addictions Program grant to the BC Centre on Substance Use to implement and evaluate a drug-checking pilot (Arrangement 1718-HQ-000024); M.E.S. held a Michael Smith Foundation for Health Research/St Paul's Foundation Scholar Award and L.T. a Michael Smith Foundation for Health Research Scholar Award; the granting agencies had no direct role (Funding, p. 7).
funding.declared_conflicts: All authors declare no conflicts of interest (p. 7). Health Canada DAS and the Provincial Toxicology Centre provided confirmatory testing; the authors state the findings are not an endorsement of the point-of-care technologies (Acknowledgements, p. 7).
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from the University of British Columbia, the BC Centre on Substance Use, Vancouver Coastal Health, the Provincial Toxicology Centre and Health Canada's Drug Analysis Service, the two laboratories that supplied the reference results; the programme evaluated is the authors' own Health Canada-funded pilot. A flag for closer reading, not a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: Confirmatory testing of all, or a random sample, of the strip-tested samples with a broad (untargeted) and quantitative method, on several strip lots, so that detection of each NPS benzodiazepine, the causes of strip false positives and the effect of dissolution could be estimated without verification bias.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: Drug-checking samples at harm-reduction sites are a fair frame for what service clients bring, not for the drug market (authors' limitation).
A convenience subset (discarded, unclaimed or client-requested samples) plus samples sent because of suspected benzodiazepine overdose.
159 confirmed samples with 24 positives; the 95% interval around the strips' 62.5% sensitivity runs from about 43% to 79% (editors' calculation).

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Sites, period, expected drug, laboratory methods and a flow diagram are given.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: Only 159 of 1368 point-of-care-tested samples (11.6%) were verified; one confirmatory sample is unaccounted for between Fig. 1 and the text.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: Forensic and toxicology laboratories with GC–MS, LC-QTOF/MS and qNMR, but targeted methods may miss the newest compounds (authors), and the target lists are in an unread supplement.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: Two laboratories with different methods, chosen by availability or site; 2 of 7 positive samples tested at both were positive at only one.
Rate formulas are correct and re-derive from Table 3, but no intervals are given and one percentage is misprinted (70.1% for 17 of 24).

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low rate managed
domains.note: Samples, not respondents; partial verification is covered under items 2 and 5.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: JBI-prevalence fits the first aim (the number and type of NPS benzodiazepines among confirmed samples) and the cross-sectional design. Judged as a test-accuracy analysis, the same problems — partial, non-random verification (159 of 1368), selection partly on suspected benzodiazepine overdose, a targeted two-laboratory reference that disagreed on 2 of 7 duplicate samples, and 24 confirmed positives — put the false-positive and false-negative rates at high risk of bias in directions that cannot be predicted. Citable for: strips and FTIR missed a substantial share of NPS benzodiazepines, especially etizolam; strips read positive in samples with no benzodiazepine found; strips detected typical benzodiazepines in six samples; etizolam was the commonest NPS benzodiazepine in this setting. Not citable for: precise accuracy figures, prevalence in the market, or accuracy elsewhere or with other strip lots.

key_findings.finding: Flow: 6156 samples submitted; 1379 tested by benzodiazepine strips and 1368 also by FTIR; 543 sent for confirmatory testing; 159 had both point-of-care and confirmatory results (120 to Health Canada DAS, 65 to the Provincial Toxicology Centre, 26 to both); 383 confirmatory-only samples had no strip test.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph; Fig. 1 (counts read from the figure image); Results › NPS benzodiazepines in confirmatory-only subsample
key_findings.note: 159 + 383 = 542, one fewer than the 543 in Fig. 1 and the text; the gap is not explained.

key_findings.finding: 24 of 159 samples (15.1%) contained at least one NPS benzodiazepine: etizolam 18, flualprazolam 4, flubromazolam 3, flubromazepam 1 (two samples held two). None was expected by the person to be an NPS benzodiazepine; they were expected to be fentanyl (15), alprazolam (5), an unknown opioid (2), heroin (1) or unknown (1).
key_findings.locator: Results › NPS benzodiazepines in primary sample, 1st paragraph; Tables 1–2

key_findings.finding: Of 114 samples expected to be opioids, 18 (15.8%) contained an NPS benzodiazepine and 16 (14.0%) both an NPS benzodiazepine and an opioid, always fentanyl; of all 24 positives, 17 contained fentanyl (one also carfentanil).
key_findings.locator: Results › NPS benzodiazepines and opioids, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Printed as 17 (70.1%); 17/24 is 70.8% (editors' calculation). Repeated in the Discussion (p. 6).

key_findings.finding: Six of the 159 samples (3.8%) contained only typical benzodiazepines (alprazolam, temazepam), all detected by the strips; they were removed from the NPS-benzodiazepine accuracy analysis, leaving 153.
key_findings.locator: Results › Point-of-care accuracy & error, 1st paragraph; Table 3 note

key_findings.finding: Strips: 15 of 24 confirmed NPS-benzodiazepine samples positive (62.5%), false-negative rate 37.5%; 20 of 129 confirmed negatives positive, false-positive rate 15.5%. Detection 87.5% (7 of 8) when flualprazolam, flubromazolam or flubromazepam was present and 50.0% (8 of 16) with etizolam alone.
key_findings.locator: Results › Point-of-care accuracy & error, 3rd paragraph; Table 3 (p. 5)
key_findings.note: The 129 confirmed negatives are the editors' sum of Table 3 counts (20 + 109); the paper gives the rates and the counts, not the total.

key_findings.finding: FTIR: 2 of 24 detected (false-negative rate 91.7%); 5 of 129 negatives positive (false-positive rate 3.9%); the two detections were etizolam samples that were negative on strips.
key_findings.locator: Results › Point-of-care accuracy & error, 4th paragraph; Table 3 (p. 5)

key_findings.finding: Either method positive: 17 of 24 detected (false-negative rate 29.2%); 23 of 129 negatives positive (false-positive rate 17.8%).
key_findings.locator: Results › Point-of-care accuracy & error, 2nd paragraph; Table 3 (p. 5)

key_findings.finding: Confirmatory-only subset: 10 of 383 (2.6%) contained NPS benzodiazepines (9 etizolam, 1 etizolam with flualprazolam), all with a high-potency opioid (fentanyl 3, carfentanil 4, both 2, fentanyl with furanyl UF-17 1); FTIR was negative for NPS benzodiazepines in all ten. In all, 34 of 543 confirmatory samples (6.3%) contained NPS benzodiazepines.
key_findings.locator: Results › NPS benzodiazepines in confirmatory-only subsample, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Of 7 NPS-benzodiazepine-positive samples sent to both confirmatory laboratories, 5 (71.4%) were confirmed at both and 2 (28.6%) at only one.

Editors' count from Table 2 (the 24 positive samples): FTIR listed caffeine in all 19 samples in which the laboratory found caffeine, but fentanyl (or fentanyl or analogue) in 3 of 17 with fentanyl, methamphetamine in 1 of 10, phenacetin in none of 7, and an NPS benzodiazepine in 2 of 24.
key_findings.note: A selected set of samples; FTIR results for fentanyl in the whole programme are not reported.

key_findings.finding: Strip used: BTNX Rapid Response single-drug benzodiazepine strip, oxazepam calibrator, cut-off 300 ng/mL, validated by the maker for 22 benzodiazepines in urine; added to the programme in October 2018 after counterfeit alprazolam containing fentanyl but no benzodiazepine was found. A BCCSU report (Shapiro et al., 2020) found flualprazolam and flubromazolam detected at concentrations similar to alprazolam, etizolam at higher concentrations, and no cross-reaction with fentanyl.

Authors' limitations: voluntary service may not represent the market; small subsamples may misestimate the rates; strips are designed for urine metabolites of common benzodiazepines (oxazepam, nordiazepam) and not for NPS benzodiazepines or dissolved drug; etizolam is reportedly insoluble in water; FTIR has difficulty with small quantities in mixtures; targeted confirmatory assays may miss the newest compounds.
The authors conclude that the substantial false-positive and false-negative rates call for cautious use of combined point-of-care methods routinely paired with confirmatory drug checking.

reporting_issues.issue: 17 of the 24 NPS-benzodiazepine-positive samples are reported as 70.1%; 17/24 is 70.8%. The same figure is repeated in the Discussion.
Fig. 1 and the text give 543 confirmatory samples, but the two subsets reported (159 with point-of-care results and 383 without strip testing) add to 542.
reporting_issues.consequence: One sample is unaccounted for; the 6.3% overall positivity (34 of 543) is unaffected in practice.

reporting_issues.issue: Fentanyl strips were part of the point-of-care testing (Abstract › Methods; Methods), but no fentanyl-strip results are reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: Selective reporting relative to the testing done; the paper cannot be cited for fentanyl-strip performance.

reporting_issues.issue: The 20 strip false positives are defined against NPS benzodiazepines only (samples with only typical benzodiazepines removed), and what they contained, or what made them react, is not reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: The false-positive rate cannot be linked to any cross-reacting compound.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 3 the 'Either' column under negative results (n = 151) counts samples negative on at least one method, while the combined false-negative rate in the text uses the 'Both' negative column (n = 113).
reporting_issues.consequence: Easy to misread; the combined false-negative rate is 7 of 24 (29.2%).
